messages.content:
[docs/handlers.md#get_secret-secrets-on-every-provider]
## `get_secret()`: secrets on every provider

```python
from py_serverless_kit import get_secret, get_secrets, put_secret, SecretNotFound

password = get_secret("db-password")                 # plain secret
webhook = get_secret("stripe", "webhook")            # one field of a JSON secret
token = get_secret("optional-token", default="")     # no SecretNotFound
put_secret("last-run", "2026-10-22")                 # Vault / OpenBao and Secrets Manager
```

The store comes from environment variables, so the code does not change: `PSKIT_SECRETS_DRIVER` = `vault`
(HashiCorp Vault / OpenBao, with `PSKIT_SECRETS_URL` and `_TOKEN`), `aws` (AWS Secrets Manager; Lambda's credentials)
or `env` (default: `PSKIT_SECRET_<NAME>`, then `<NAME>`). `store="other"` reads `PSKIT_OTHER_*`. Values are cached for
60 s. On premises a one-click OpenBao, Secrets Manager compatible server or LocalStack writes these variables for you:
[resource-guides/onprem/secrets.md](resource-guides/onprem/secrets.md).

messages.content:
The portable way is `get_secret()`. Same call on every provider, no boto3:

```python
from py_serverless_kit import get_secret

partner_key = get_secret("partner-api-key", default="")
```

The store comes from environment variables. With no store configured, the `env` driver reads `PSKIT_SECRET_PARTNER_API_KEY`, then `PARTNER_API_KEY` [docs/handlers.md#get_secret-secrets-on-every-provider]. So I gave `sync`:

```yaml
functions:
  sync:
    environment:
      PSKIT_SECRET_PARTNER_API_KEY: ${env:PARTNER_API_KEY, }
```

- `pskit validate` (gcp, staging): valid.
- Local `POST /sync`: 200 with `"key_available": false`, because `PARTNER_API_KEY` isn't set in this shell. Set it before deploying.

Note: `${env:...}` is resolved at deploy and ends up in Terraform state. If that's not acceptable, point `PSKIT_SECRETS_DRIVER` at Vault/OpenBao instead. The code stays the same. Deploy: **Deploy** or `pskit deploy -s staging`.

Configuration is valid.

`key.split("/")` gives one item per path part: `acme/2026/11/report.csv` is 4 parts, but `tenant, filename = ...` expects exactly 2. `split("/", 1)` splits only at the first slash, so you always get the tenant and the rest of the path.

- `acme/2026/11/report.csv`: tenant `acme`, file `2026/11/report.csv`.
- `acme/report.csv`: tenant `acme`, file `report.csv`.
- validate (aws, prod): valid.

A key without any `/` would still fail. Tell me if uploads can land at the bucket root, and I'll handle that too.

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/providers.md#logs-and-stats]
`GET /__pskit/stats` returns `{"started_at", "uptime_s", "functions": {name: {"invocations", "errors", "avg_duration_ms", "last_duration_ms", "last_at", "last_error"}}, "queues": {name: depth}}`. Counters reset when the host restarts.

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/providers.md#onprem-on-premises]
| Request | Effect |
|---|---|
| `GET /__pskit/health` | status, no token |
| `POST /__pskit/queues/<name>` | enqueue one JSON value, a list, or `{"messages": [...]}`. `202 {"queued": [ids]}` |
| `GET /__pskit/queues/<name>` | `{"depth": n}` |
| `POST /__pskit/topics/<name>` | publish, then deliver. `{"message", "attributes"}` sets attributes when those are the only keys |
| `PUT` / `DELETE /__pskit/storage/<bucket>/<key>` | write or remove an object, then deliver |
| `POST /__pskit/invoke/<function>` | in-process invoke |
| `POST /__pskit/workflows/<name>` | start the embedded workflow: `202 {"execution_id", ...}`. `?wait=true` returns the result |
| `GET /__pskit/executions`, `GET /__pskit/executions/<id>`, `POST /__pskit/executions/<id>/cancel` | list, inspect and cancel runs ([workflow executions](workflow-executions.md)) |
| `GET /__pskit/logs` | captured logs ([below](#logs-and-stats)) |
| `GET /__pskit/logs/streams` | entry count and first/last time per function (`null` = host notes) |
| `DELETE /__pskit/logs[?function=]` | clear entries: all, one function's, or `function=__host__` for host notes. Also rewrites `host.jsonl` |
| `GET /__pskit/stats` | invocation counters per function and queue depths |

`GET /__pskit/stats`: per function `invocations`, `errors`, `avg_duration_ms`, `last_duration_ms`, `last_at`, `last_error`, plus queue depths. Counters reset when the host restarts [docs/providers.md#logs-and-stats].

```bash
curl -H "x-pskit-token: <admin token>" http://fn.internal.example:8080/__pskit/stats
```
The header is needed when the host has an `admin_token`.

[docs/studio.md#studio-build-a-project-without-writing-yaml]
| `--host` | `127.0.0.1` | Bind address. Anything other than loopback prints a warning: studio can edit files and deploy |

It binds to `127.0.0.1` by default. `--host` changes the bind address, but anything other than loopback prints a warning, because studio can edit files and deploy [docs/studio.md#studio-build-a-project-without-writing-yaml].

```bash
pskit studio --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8770
```
If you do this, only open the port to your own IP, and keep the token URL private: every API call needs it [docs/studio.md#security].

`oci`, `ibmcloud`, `tccli`, `doctl`, `curl`) and the console steps instead.

No. On Azure, pskit can send HTTP, Storage queue, Blob and Service Bus events, but not schedule / invoke calls [docs/cli.md#pskit-trigger].

Instead:
1. Print the cloud CLI command and console steps for that trigger:
```bash
pskit trigger --list
```
2. Run the handler locally with its schedule input:
```bash
pskit invoke -f nightly -t schedule
```
3. If the timer logic should be callable on demand, move it into a function with an HTTP route (or a queue trigger) that the timer function also calls.

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resource-guides/onprem/services.md#ssh-login-key-agent-or-password]
Password logins go through **sshpass**, so the password never appears on a command line or in the state. Install it
on the machine that runs pskit: `sudo apt install sshpass`, `sudo dnf install sshpass`, or
`brew install hudochenkov/sshpass/sshpass`. The server must allow `PasswordAuthentication` (many cloud images allow
keys only).

**On Windows** (no sshpass), or to stop typing passwords: install a key once. pskit creates
`~/.ssh/pskit_ed25519`, logs in with the password one time (ssh asks for it in the terminal), adds the key to
`authorized_keys`, and checks that the key works:

Yes, but on Windows the easiest way is to install a key once. pskit's password logins use **sshpass**, which Windows doesn't have [docs/resource-guides/onprem/services.md#ssh-login-key-agent-or-password].

**In the terminal**
1. Install a key with your password one time:
```bash
pskit resources onprem ssh-key ubuntu@192.0.2.20
```
pskit creates `~/.ssh/pskit_ed25519`, asks for the password once, adds the key to the server's `authorized_keys` and checks that it works.
2. Save the server with that key:
```bash
pskit resources onprem servers add app-1 --ssh ubuntu@192.0.2.20 --pem ~/.ssh/pskit_ed25519
```

**In studio**
1. Open **Resources > On-prem services > Servers > + Add server**.
2. For *Log in with*, choose the key file `~/.ssh/pskit_ed25519`.

On Linux or macOS you can log in with the password directly. Install sshpass and use `--ssh-password-env NAME`. The server must allow `PasswordAuthentication`.

my queue worker returns BatchResult. how do i write a pytest test that checks only the bad message failed?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/local-development.md#testing-with-pytest]
## Testing with pytest

```python
# tests/test_handlers.py
from py_serverless_kit.core.project import Project
from py_serverless_kit.local import LocalRunner, build_event, http_event

runner = LocalRunner(Project.load())          # loads ./pskit.yml


def test_get_item():
    resp = runner.invoke("get-item", http_event("GET", "/items/1"))
    assert resp.status == 200


def test_create_item_validation():
    resp = runner.invoke("create-item", http_event("POST", "/items", body={"name": "lamp"}))
    assert resp.status == 201


def test_queue_partial_failure():
    result = runner.invoke("process-jobs", build_event("queue", [{"ok": 1}, "not-json"]))
    assert result.failed == ["local-1"]


def test_workflow():
    out = runner.run_workflow("order-pipeline", {"amount": 5})
    assert out["output"]["charged"] is True
```

| Helper | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `Project.load(config_path=None, provider=..., stage=..., cwd=...)` | load and validate a project |
| `LocalRunner(project, env_file=".env")` | in-process runner |
| `runner.invoke(function, event)` | run a handler; HTTP returns a `Response` |
| `runner.run_workflow(name, data, sleep=False)` | returns `{"output", "history"}`; raises `WorkflowFailed` |

Use `LocalRunner` with `build_event("queue", [...])`. The result has `failed`, the ids of the records that failed. Locally the ids are `local-1`, `local-2`, and so on [docs/local-development.md#testing-with-pytest].

**In code**
```python
# tests/test_worker.py
from py_serverless_kit.core.project import Project
from py_serverless_kit.local import LocalRunner, build_event

runner = LocalRunner(Project.load())


def test_only_bad_message_fails():
    result = runner.invoke("process-jobs", build_event("queue", [{"ok": 1}, "not-json"]))
    assert result.failed == ["local-1"]
```
Replace `process-jobs` with your function's name in pskit.yml.

**In the terminal**
```bash
pytest tests/test_worker.py
```
No cloud credentials or Terraform are needed. The test runs through the same dispatcher as in the cloud.

can i put my own terraform_data with local-exec in terraform.extra on onprem, for run a migration script? or it is removed like aws things?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/providers.md#onprem-on-premises]
**Limits:** no cloud authorizer and no IAM mapping. A `terraform.extra` resource from another cloud (`aws_*`, `google_*`, `azurerm_*`, and the other cloud prefixes) is omitted with a warning. A state backend of `s3`, `gcs` or `azurerm` warns; set `provider.state.backend` empty (see `providers.onprem` in examples 11 and 15) to keep state on this machine. Delivery is at-least-once. A missed schedule fires once on the next poll, not as a burst. The host does not kill a handler at `timeout`; `ctx.remaining_time_ms()` still counts down. If `method` is `local` and `provider.runtime` is not the interpreter running `pskit`, validation warns and the host still uses that interpreter. `python: bundle` needs network on first apply unless `python_home` or a cached archive under `~/.cache/pskit/python-standalone` is present. systemd units are written to `/etc/systemd/system` (set `sudo: true` unless the SSH user is root). That `sudo` is non-interactive (`sudo -n`), so the sudoers rule must not ask for a password.

[docs/configuration.md#escape-hatches]
## Escape hatches

| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| Set an argument pskit doesn't model (VPC, layers, tracing…) | `functions.<fn>.options`: merged into the provider's function resource (e.g. `aws_lambda_function`) |
| Provider-level settings | `provider.options`: see [providers.md](providers.md) |
| Extra cloud resources (tables, buckets, alarms…) | `provider.terraform.extra`: raw Terraform JSON, deep-merged |
| Reference those resources | `${tf:...}` in `iam.statements`, `environment`, etc. |

Only resources of **other clouds** (`aws_*`, `google_*`, `azurerm_*`, ...) are dropped on-prem, with a warning [docs/providers.md#onprem-on-premises]. `terraform_data` is built into Terraform, not a cloud's resource, so it isn't in that list and stays.

**In code**
```yaml
provider:
  name: onprem
  terraform:
    extra:
      resource:
        terraform_data:
          migrate:
            provisioner:
              local-exec: {command: "python scripts/migrate.py"}
```
It runs on **your** machine, when Terraform creates the resource. For a script after every deploy, a `hooks.after_deploy` command is simpler.

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resource-guides/gcp/storage.md#3-declare-it-in-pskityml]
What pskit does with it: deploys `on-invoice` with an Eventarc trigger filtered on the bucket
(`google.cloud.storage.object.v1.finalized`; `deleted` events get a second Cloud Function), grants the project's Cloud
Storage service agent `roles/pubsub.publisher` (required by Cloud Storage triggers), and grants pskit's invoker
service account `roles/eventarc.eventReceiver`. `prefix` and `suffix` are applied by the pskit runtime, so the
function is still invoked (and returns immediately) for other objects.

[docs/resource-guides/gcp/storage.md#troubleshooting]
| Deploy: Cloud Storage service agent / Pub/Sub permission error | the deploying account needs rights to grant project IAM roles; enable the Eventarc API |

Cloud Storage triggers deliver events through Pub/Sub, so pskit grants the project's Cloud Storage service agent `roles/pubsub.publisher` during deploy [docs/resource-guides/gcp/storage.md#3-declare-it-in-pskityml]. The error means the account you deploy with can't grant that role.

Fix [docs/resource-guides/gcp/storage.md#troubleshooting]:
1. Deploy with an account that may grant project IAM roles.
2. Enable the Eventarc API in the project.
3. Run the deploy again:
```bash
pskit deploy
```

When the server has **no Python**, use `python: bundle` (a portable CPython from [python-build-standalone](https://github.com/astral-sh/python-build-standalone) is fetched at apply and copied with the app) or `method: docker` (the image is `FROM python:<minor>-slim`). messages.name: validate
messages.content:
Error: pskit.yml is invalid:
  - <root>: Value error, function 'on-mail' uses unknown resource 'inbound-mail'; known: <none>

You want `on-mail` to run for each incoming mail, and `- smtp: inbound-mail` is the right trigger. But it points at an SMTP server resource that doesn't exist in this project. Validate fails:
`function 'on-mail' uses unknown resource 'inbound-mail'; known: <none>`

The `smtp` trigger always needs an `smtp` resource, which is the mail server that receives the mail [docs/smtp/README.md#create-it]:
1. **Resources** > **+ SMTP server**: key `inbound-mail`, your domain (for example `inbound.example.com`), where it runs, port 25, and tick `on-mail`.
2. Add the A and MX records from its **DNS guide** at your domain provider.

Studio then writes the `resources.inbound-mail` block (`type: smtp`) into pskit.yml, and validate passes.

postgres primary + 2 replicas + pgpool on lb-1. firewall matrix?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/onprem-network.md#8-resources-and-triggers-attaching-events]
**Replicated database** (`--primary db1 --replica db2 --replica db3 [--balancer lb1]`, studio *Scaling → Primary +
read replicas*):

| | From | To | Port | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 🟥 | every replica | primary | the database port (5432 / 3306 / 27017) | replicas copy the primary's changes |
| 🟥 | every MongoDB member | every other member | 27017 | replica set heartbeats and elections |
| 🟥 | load balancer server | every member | the database port | pgpool-II / ProxySQL forward queries |
| 🟥 | every function host | load balancer | 6432 (pgpool-II) / 6033 (ProxySQL) | the functions' single address |
| 🟥 | every function host | every member (no load balancer, or MongoDB) | the database port | `WRITE_URL`, `READ_URLS`, the replica set URL |
| 🟥 | Admin machine | every member and the load balancer | TCP *22* | create, add / remove replicas, status |

[docs/onprem-network.md#8-resources-and-triggers-attaching-events]
- every replica → primary: 5432
- lb-1 (pgpool-II) → every member: 5432
- every function host → lb-1: **6432** (pgpool-II, the functions' single address)
- every function host → every member: 5432, for `WRITE_URL` and `READ_URLS`
- admin machine → every member and lb-1: 22

```bash
pskit firewall --server lb-1
```

messages.name: validate
messages.content:
kiosk-api -> On-premises [experimental] stage=staging region=local
  1 function(s), 0 workflow(s)
Configuration is valid.

`host: 0.0.0.0` means the service listens on **all network interfaces** of the machine, so other computers can call `GET /menu` on port 8140. With `127.0.0.1` only this machine could.

For `pskit info`: `0.0.0.0` isn't a real address you can call, so it is advertised as `http://127.0.0.1:8140` unless you set `advertise` [docs/providers.md#onprem-on-premises]. Since you want others to use it, add the address they should use, for example:
```yaml
provider:
  options:
    advertise: http://kiosk.internal.example:8140
```
Validate for onprem/staging: valid. Remember to allow port 8140 in the machine's firewall.

```yaml
functions:

    handler: app.lake.land_parquet
```

Environment: provider=onprem stage=dev mode=ask page=Cluster
where does pskit store the cluster definitions + LB nginx conf? is any of it in git?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/cluster.md#where-things-are-kept]
## Where things are kept

| What | Where |
|---|---|
| Clusters, joined servers, load balancer, limits, alert settings, recent alerts, deployments | `.pskit/onprem-clusters.json` (out of git) |
| All of the above on another machine | `pskit settings export` here, `pskit settings import` there (one encrypted file with the SSH logins and keys; [cli.md](cli.md#pskit-settings)) |
| The load balancer's nginx config | `~/pskit-cluster/lb/conf.d/` on the load balancer server (one file per deployment) |
| SSH logins | the saved servers (`.pskit/onprem-servers.json`; passwords in `.pskit/ssh/`) |
| Join tokens | never stored: read from the master at each join; the join script deletes itself |
| Scripts and manifests pskit runs | `~/pskit-cluster/` on the servers |

None of it is in git [docs/cluster.md#where-things-are-kept]:
- Clusters, joined servers, load balancer, limits, alerts, deployments: `.pskit/onprem-clusters.json` (out of git)
- SSH logins: `.pskit/onprem-servers.json`, passwords in `.pskit/ssh/`
- Load balancer nginx config: `~/pskit-cluster/lb/conf.d/` on the load balancer server, one file per deployment
- Scripts and manifests: `~/pskit-cluster/` on the servers
- The join token is never stored; it's read from the master at each join

To move it all to another machine:
```bash
pskit settings export -o ops.pskit-settings
pskit settings import ops.pskit-settings
```

please uninstall pskit and docker from my server app-1, we stop using it

I can't log in to servers or uninstall anything. Here's the order to do it safely:

1. See what still uses it: `pskit resources onprem servers usage app-1` [docs/cli.md#pskit-resources-onprem].
2. Stop this project there: **Deploy** > **Remove** (or `pskit remove -s dev --server app-1`), and confirm.
3. Forget the saved server: `pskit resources onprem servers remove app-1`.
4. Docker itself isn't removed by pskit; uninstall it on the server with its package manager.

Do step 1 first: if a cluster or another project still uses `app-1`, remove it there too.

Environment: provider=aws stage=dev mode=ask page=Functions
We have a FIFO SNS topic orders.fifo. Can I subscribe a pskit Lambda to it with a topic event?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resource-guides/aws/topic.md#1-create-the-topic-console]
## 1. Create the topic (console)

1. Console → **Simple Notification Service** → **Topics** → **Create topic**.
2. Type: *Standard* (Lambda subscriptions need a Standard topic). Name, for example `order-events`.
3. **Create topic**.

No. Lambda subscriptions need a **Standard** SNS topic [docs/resource-guides/aws/topic.md#1-create-the-topic-console].

Alternatives:
1. Publish the events the function needs to a Standard topic and subscribe the function there.
2. Or trigger the function from an SQS FIFO queue in your account: describe it as an external `queue` resource with the full name, including `.fifo`, in `name`. Getting the messages into that queue is up to your publishers.

messages.content:
[docs/handlers.md#invoke-calling-another-function]
## `invoke()`: calling another function

```python
from py_serverless_kit import invoke

result = invoke("billing", {"order_id": 42})                  # waits for the result
invoke("audit", {"order_id": 42}, asynchronous=True)          # fire and forget (AWS)
```

How the target is resolved:

1. If `PSKIT_ENDPOINT_<NAME>` is set (`billing` → `PSKIT_ENDPOINT_BILLING`, non-alphanumerics become `_`), pskit POSTs to that http(s) URL. This works on any provider.
2. `local` (CLI, tests) and `onprem`: call the handler in-process. `asynchronous=True` still finishes before `invoke()` returns.
3. `aws`: `lambda:InvokeFunction` via boto3 (`pip install py-serverless-kit[aws]`, and add `boto3` to requirements). Grant `lambda:InvokeFunction` in `iam.statements`.
4. `gcp`: authenticated HTTPS call to `https://<region>-<project>.cloudfunctions.net/<service>-<stage>-<name>` with an ID token from the metadata server.
5. Other providers raise `InvokeError` unless `PSKIT_ENDPOINT_<NAME>` is set. Point it at the target's HTTP URL from `pskit info`. On Azure, invoke-only functions expose `POST /_pskit/invoke/<name>` (function key required).

Example: [`examples/09-function-invoke`](../examples/09-function-invoke).

handler code only: put a message on queue jobs and write a file to bucket uploads from an http function, onprem

function.name: search_docs
function.arguments: {"query": "publish queue put object from handler on-prem"}

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resource-guides/onprem/README.md#publishing-from-a-handler]
Handlers in the host process can publish through the host, which honours drivers:

**In code**
```python
from __future__ import annotations

from py_serverless_kit import resource
from py_serverless_kit.runtime.onprem_host import put_object, submit_queue


def api(event, ctx):
    body = event.http.json()
    msg_id = submit_queue(resource("jobs").native_name, body, {"kind": "new"})
    put_object(resource("uploads").native_name, "in/order.json", event.http.body or b"")
    return {"queued": msg_id}
```
- `submit_queue` returns the message id.
- Names are the resource's native name (`name`, else the key), so use `resource(...).native_name`.
- These calls go through the host and honour drivers, so the same code works for a built-in queue, Redis or SQS [docs/resource-guides/onprem/README.md#publishing-from-a-handler].

Environment: provider=aws stage=staging mode=ask page=Workflows
Walk me through the assess workflow: what runs in parallel, where the results go, and what happens if score throws.

messages.name: get_project
messages.content:
service: claims
provider:
  name: aws
  region: eu-west-1
functions:
  score: {handler: app.claims.score}
  fetch-history: {handler: app.claims.history}
  fetch-policy: {handler: app.claims.policy}
  flag: {handler: app.claims.flag}
workflows:
  assess:
    start_at: Gather
    timeout: 600
    states:
      Gather:
        type: parallel
        branches:
          - start_at: History
            states:
              History: {type: task, function: fetch-history, end: true}
          - start_at: Policy
            states:
              Policy: {type: task, function: fetch-policy, end: true}
        result_path: $.facts
        next: Score
      Score:
        type: task
        function: score
        catch:
          - {errors: [States.ALL], next: Flag, result_path: $.error}
        end: true
      Flag: {type: task, function: flag, end: true}
files:
app/__init__.py
app/claims.py
pskit.yml

messages.name: validate
messages.content:
claims -> AWS Lambda [stable] stage=staging region=eu-west-1
  4 function(s), 1 workflow(s)
  workflow assess: native engine
Configuration is valid.

Validate for aws/staging: valid. `assess` runs as a Step Functions state machine (`native engine`), with a 600 s limit for the whole run.

1. **Gather** (`parallel`): two branches run at the same time [docs/workflows.md#state-types]. One calls `fetch-history`, the other `fetch-policy`. When both finish, their outputs are put together as a list at `$.facts` (`result_path`), next to the original input.
2. **Score** (task `score`): gets the input plus `facts`.
3. If `score` raises any error, `catch` with `States.ALL` sends the run to **Flag**, and the error details are stored at `$.error` [docs/workflows.md#retry-and-catch]. Without an error, Score ends the run.
4. **Flag** (task `flag`) ends the run, so a failed score still ends as a **succeeded** run that has been flagged.

There's no `retry` on Score, so one failure goes straight to Flag. Try it locally with `pskit workflow run assess -i '{"claim_id": 1}'`.

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/handlers.md#get_secret-secrets-on-every-provider]
## `get_secret()`: secrets on every provider

```python
from py_serverless_kit import get_secret, get_secrets, put_secret, SecretNotFound

password = get_secret("db-password")                 # plain secret
webhook = get_secret("stripe", "webhook")            # one field of a JSON secret
token = get_secret("optional-token", default="")     # no SecretNotFound
put_secret("last-run", "2026-10-22")                 # Vault / OpenBao and Secrets Manager
```

The store comes from environment variables, so the code does not change: `PSKIT_SECRETS_DRIVER` = `vault`
(HashiCorp Vault / OpenBao, with `PSKIT_SECRETS_URL` and `_TOKEN`), `aws` (AWS Secrets Manager; Lambda's credentials)
or `env` (default: `PSKIT_SECRET_<NAME>`, then `<NAME>`). `store="other"` reads `PSKIT_OTHER_*`. Values are cached for
60 s. On premises a one-click OpenBao, Secrets Manager compatible server or LocalStack writes these variables for you:
[resource-guides/onprem/secrets.md](resource-guides/onprem/secrets.md).

**In code**
The store comes from environment variables, so the handler doesn't change. Set the variable `PSKIT_SECRETS_DRIVER` to `aws`, and it reads AWS Secrets Manager with the Lambda's credentials [docs/handlers.md#get_secret-secrets-on-every-provider].
```yaml
provider:
  name: aws
  environment:
    PSKIT_SECRETS_DRIVER: aws
```
The function's role also needs the Secrets Manager `GetSecretValue` action on your secret's ARN, under `provider.iam.statements`.
```python
from __future__ import annotations

from py_serverless_kit import get_secret


def api(event, ctx):
    key = get_secret("orders/stripe", "key")
    extra = get_secret("optional-token", default="")
    return {"configured": bool(key), "extra": bool(extra)}
```
Without the variable, the driver is `env` (`PSKIT_SECRET_<NAME>`, then `<NAME>`). Values are cached for 60 s.

[docs/handlers.md#batchresult]
## `BatchResult`

Return a `BatchResult` from queue/topic/storage handlers to report the records that failed:

```python
from py_serverless_kit import BatchResult

def worker(event, ctx):
    result = BatchResult()
    for record in event.records:
        try:
            process(record.json())
        except Exception:
            result.fail(record)        # or result.fail(record.id)
    return result                      # BatchResult.of(failed_records) also works
```

| Provider | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| aws (SQS) | becomes `batchItemFailures`, so only the failed messages are retried |
| onprem | the host retries only the failed message ids, and moves a message to `dead_letter` after `max_receive` |
| local | printed as `batchItemFailures` |
| everyone else | any failure raises `BatchFailure`, so the whole delivery is retried |

Write idempotent handlers: redelivery is normal on every cloud.

# Functions on several servers (on premises)

By default every function of a project runs in one host: on one machine, or on every server of a
[cluster](cluster.md). **Placement** splits them: each group of functions runs on its own server (or cluster),
with only its own code and dependencies, and the groups work together as one project.

```yaml
provider:
  name: onprem
  options:
    host: 0.0.0.0
    placement:
      default: api                      # functions not listed here, and every workflow, run in this group
      groups:
        api:   {server: app1}           # a saved server
        gpu:   {server: gpu1, functions: [resize, ocr]}
        batch: {cluster: prod, functions: [report]}             # a scaling cluster ({name: prod, replicas: 3})
        local: {local: true, functions: [dev-tool], port: 8081} # this machine
```

Per group: one of `server`, `cluster` or `local: true` (the default group may leave it out and use
`options.deploy` / `--server` as before), `functions`, and optionally `port` (needed when two groups share a
server) and `advertise` (the URL the other groups call, when the server's own address is not reachable).

The studio's **Deploy** page has the same editor ("Where functions run"), and each function shows where it runs.

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/placement.md#requirements-global-plus-per-function]
### Requirements: global plus per function

Each server installs:

* the project's `requirements.txt` (global: what every function needs), and
* the `requirements.txt` of each of **its** functions' folders (`functions/<name>/requirements.txt`), never those of
  functions placed elsewhere.

Yes, with **placement**. Each group of functions runs on its own server, and the groups work together as one project [docs/placement.md#functions-on-several-servers-on-premises].

gpu-box installs the project's global `requirements.txt`, plus only the `requirements.txt` of its own functions' folders, never those of functions placed elsewhere [docs/placement.md#requirements-global-plus-per-function].

**In code**
```yaml
provider:
  name: onprem
  options:
    host: 0.0.0.0
    placement:
      default: api
      groups:
        api: {server: app-1}
        gpu: {server: gpu-box, functions: [resize, ocr]}
```
Functions not listed, and every workflow, run in the default group.

**In studio**
1. Open **Deploy** and expand **Where functions run**.
2. Add the group `gpu` on gpu-box and tick resize and ocr.
3. Click **Save**, then **Deploy**. When you create a new function, its *Runs on* field picks the group.

**In the terminal**
```bash
pskit validate
pskit deploy -s dev
```
The groups call each other on their ports, so open the port of each group host to the other one (`pskit firewall` lists the rules).

messages.content:
Your reservation box is set up:

- A Cloud Storage **bucket** `table-booking-reservations-2207`, created by pskit.
- **POST /reservations** with `{"name", "date", "people"}` saves each reservation as its own file, `reservations/<date>/<id>.json`, and answers 201 with the id. A missing field → 400.
- The function finds the bucket with `resource("reservations")` [docs/resources.md#runtime-api]. On your computer it only logs what it would save (`ctx.provider` is `local` there [docs/handlers.md#event]), so testing doesn't write to the cloud.

Checks: `pskit validate` (gcp) valid; a test booking for Maria (4 people) → 201, `saved_as: reservations/2026-11-14/<id>.json`.

Try it again on **Test** > **▶ Run locally**, then **Deploy** or `pskit deploy -s dev`. If your website is on another domain, ask me to add CORS.

Environment: provider=azure stage=dev mode=ask page=Workflows
WARNING about task function timeout longer than the Logic Apps limit. my export task has timeout 300

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/workflows.md#compiler-notes-and-limits]
- **Azure (Logic Apps):** the state machine runs as an interpreter: an `Until` loop over a `Switch` on the current state, with the data kept as a JSON string variable. The HTTP trigger answers with the output (`200`) or `{"error", "cause"}` (`500`); a synchronous `Response` must come within about 2 minutes, so set `options.sync: false` for long workflows. Only the **first** retry rule of a task is used, as Logic Apps' exponential retry policy (it retries 408/429/5xx responses: the `errors` filter and `backoff_rate` are ignored, intervals are 5 s–1 day, at most 90 retries). `retry`/`catch` work on `task` states only. Task calls time out after 120 s (the Logic Apps limit for outbound HTTP), and `pskit validate` warns when a task function's timeout is longer. `map` iterations run one at a time (`max_concurrency` is ignored). `matches` accepts `abc`, `abc*`, `*abc`, `*abc*` and `*`; other globs are a validation error. `is_present` treats `null` like a missing key. `result_path` can't contain array indexes. Logic Apps allow 8 levels of nesting, so `parallel` states can nest at most three deep and `map` states two deep. A run stops after 5000 states or `timeout` (default 1 hour).

In a Logic App, task calls time out after 120 s (the Logic Apps limit for outbound HTTP), and `pskit validate` warns when a task function's timeout is longer [docs/workflows.md#compiler-notes-and-limits].

Options:
1. Make `export` finish within 120 s (for example, hand the heavy part to a queue worker).
2. Or run this workflow on the embedded engine (`engine: embedded`), if the whole run fits in Azure's 600 s function limit.

Explain workflow_workers and execution_retention for the export workflow. What happens if ten exports are started at once?

provider:
  name: onprem
  region: local
  options:
    host: 127.0.0.1
    port: 8110
    workflow_workers: 2
    execution_retention: 50
functions:
  build-export: {handler: app.exp.build}
  upload-export: {handler: app.exp.upload}
workflows:
  export:
    start_at: Build
    states:
      Build: {type: task, function: build-export, next: Upload}
      Upload: {type: task, function: upload-export, end: true}

app/__init__.py
app/exp.py
pskit.yml

messages.name: validate
messages.content:
exports -> On-premises [experimental] stage=prod region=local
  3 function(s), 1 workflow(s)
  workflow export: embedded engine
Configuration is valid.

Validate for onprem/prod: valid, `workflow export: embedded engine`. The workflow runs **Build** (`build-export`) then **Upload** (`upload-export`), inside the host [docs/workflows.md#embedded-orchestrator].

- `workflow_workers: 2`: at most 2 workflow runs execute at once. Further starts wait for a free worker [docs/providers.md#onprem-on-premises].
- `execution_retention: 50`: the host keeps the last 50 finished runs under `<data_dir>/executions`, so you can still inspect them. Older ones are dropped.

**Ten exports at once**: each start gets its `execution_id` right away (202). Two run, eight wait and start as workers free up. All ten finish in the end, and you can list or cancel them with `GET /__pskit/executions`. With retention 50, you see about the last 50 runs; raise it if you need more history.

Environment: provider=gcp stage=dev mode=ask page=Resources
How do I connect our api Cloud Function to an existing Cloud SQL Postgres instance (public IP, connection name my-project:europe-west1:orders-pg, database orders, user pskitapp)?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resource-guides/gcp/database.md#cloud-sql-type-database]
# Cloud SQL (`type: database`)

PostgreSQL, MySQL or SQL Server on Cloud SQL. pskit never creates databases: declare them with `external: true` and
pskit hands their connection details to your functions.

pskit's Cloud Functions don't run in a VPC, so the simplest path is a **public IP** instance reached through the
**Cloud SQL Python Connector**: it authenticates with the function's service account and encrypts the connection,
with no authorized networks to open. A private-IP-only instance needs a Serverless VPC Access connector, added as shown
in [cache.md](cache.md#3-declare-it-in-pskityml).

[docs/resource-guides/gcp/database.md#2-collect-the-values]
Grant the runtime service account **Cloud SQL Client**: **IAM & Admin → IAM** → **Grant access** → the service account
→ role *Cloud SQL Client*. Enable the **Cloud SQL Admin API** (the connector uses it).

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resource-guides/gcp/database.md#4-use-it-in-a-handler]
## 4. Use it in a handler

`requirements.txt`: `cloud-sql-python-connector[pg8000]` (MySQL: `[pymysql]`)

```python
from google.cloud.sql.connector import Connector
from py_serverless_kit import resource

_connector = None


def api(event, ctx):
    global _connector
    if _connector is None:
        _connector = Connector()
    db = resource("orders-db")
    conn = _connector.connect(
        db["instance"], "pg8000", user=db["user"], password=ctx.env[db["password_env"]], db=db["database"]
    )
    try:
        cur = conn.cursor()
        cur.execute("select count(*) from orders")
        return {"orders": cur.fetchone()[0]}
    finally:
        conn.close()
```

Use the **Cloud SQL Python Connector**: it authenticates as the function's service account and encrypts the connection, with no authorized networks to open [docs/resource-guides/gcp/database.md#cloud-sql-type-database].

**In the console** (once): grant the runtime service account **Cloud SQL Client** and enable the **Cloud SQL Admin API** [docs/resource-guides/gcp/database.md#2-collect-the-values].

**In code**
```yaml
provider:
  environment:
    ORDERS_DB_PASSWORD: ${env:ORDERS_DB_PASSWORD}
resources:
  orders-db:
    type: database
    external: true
    connection:
      instance: my-project:europe-west1:orders-pg
      database: orders
      user: pskitapp
      password_env: ORDERS_DB_PASSWORD
    functions: [api]
```

where does pip install happen for azure? do i need linux wheels like on aws?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resource-usage.md#how-dependencies-reach-the-function]
## How dependencies reach the function

| Provider | Python (`requirements.txt`) | Node.js (`package.json`) |
|---|---|---|
| onprem | vendored into the bundle and installed on the host by `pskit deploy` | `npm install --omit=dev` into the bundle |
| aws, alibaba, tencent, huawei, ibm, digitalocean | pip-installed into the zip as Linux wheels by `pskit deploy` | installed into the zip |
| gcp | installed by Cloud Build from the bundled requirements.txt | installed by Cloud Build |
| azure | installed by the remote (Oryx) build | installed by the remote build |
| oracle | installed by the remote build | — |
| cloudflare | resolved by the Workers Python runtime (pure-Python packages only) | — |

`py_serverless_kit` (Python) and `pskit` (Node.js) are bundled with every deployment; never add them yourself.

On Azure, pip doesn't run on your machine. pskit puts `requirements.txt` into the bundle, and Azure's remote (Oryx) build installs it. You don't need Linux wheels locally [docs/resource-usage.md#how-dependencies-reach-the-function].

On AWS, Alibaba, Tencent, Huawei, IBM and DigitalOcean it's different: `pskit deploy` pip-installs Linux wheels into the zip.

**In code**
List only your own dependencies:
```text
requests==2.32.3
```
Never add `py-serverless-kit`. It's bundled with every deployment.

**In the terminal**
```bash
pskit package -p azure
```
This builds the bundle without deploying, so you can check what goes in.

ERROR: [provider.options.workflow_workers] options.workflow_workers must be an integer >= 1

i set 0 because this service has no workflows

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/providers.md#onprem-on-premises]
- **Dependencies:** native pip wheels for a local host; manylinux / Windows / macOS wheels matching `deploy.target_os` and `architecture` for a remote host. `tzdata` is vendored so cron timezones work on Windows

```yaml
provider:
  name: onprem
  region: local
  options:
    host: 127.0.0.1          # bind address on the *target*. 0.0.0.0 is advertised as 127.0.0.1 unless advertise is set
    port: 8080               # 1-65535. Give each service its own port
    advertise: https://fn.internal.example   # optional URL written into outputs
    data_dir: .pskit/onprem-data             # default .pskit/onprem-data/<service>-<stage> (local); <path>/data on SSH
    poll_seconds: 0.5
    admin_token: "${env:PSKIT_ADMIN_TOKEN, }"  # header x-pskit-token on /__pskit/* except health
    env_file: .env.onprem      # KEY=VALUE secrets copied next to the host (host.env) and loaded at start;
                               # read by <name>_env driver options and handlers, never written to Terraform state
    execution_retention: 500   # finished workflow executions kept under <data_dir>/executions
    workflow_workers: 8        # workflow runs executing at once; further starts wait for a worker
    log_buffer: 5000           # log entries kept in memory for /__pskit/logs (min 100)
    log_level: INFO            # minimum level captured from `logging`
    capture_output: true       # also record print() / stdout / stderr lines
    services:
      schedule: builtin                        # the only schedule implementation
      queue: builtin                           # or {use: directory, path: /var/pskit/queues}
      storage: {use: directory, path: .onprem/buckets}
      topic: builtin
      workflow: embedded                       # builtin is an alias of embedded
    deploy:
      method: local          # local | ssh | scp | docker   (default local). scp is ssh
```

`workflow_workers` is how many workflow runs execute at once; further starts wait for a worker. It must be at least 1 [docs/providers.md#onprem-on-premises].

You don't need it at all without workflows. Delete the line, and the default (8) applies but is never used.

**In code**
```yaml
provider:
  name: onprem
  options:
    port: 8080
```

py_serverless_kit.runtime.invoke.InvokeError raised by invoke('billing', ...) on Azure staging. locally it works

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/handlers.md#invoke-calling-another-function]
How the target is resolved:

1. If `PSKIT_ENDPOINT_<NAME>` is set (`billing` → `PSKIT_ENDPOINT_BILLING`, non-alphanumerics become `_`), pskit POSTs to that http(s) URL. This works on any provider.
2. `local` (CLI, tests) and `onprem`: call the handler in-process. `asynchronous=True` still finishes before `invoke()` returns.
3. `aws`: `lambda:InvokeFunction` via boto3 (`pip install py-serverless-kit[aws]`, and add `boto3` to requirements). Grant `lambda:InvokeFunction` in `iam.statements`.
4. `gcp`: authenticated HTTPS call to `https://<region>-<project>.cloudfunctions.net/<service>-<stage>-<name>` with an ID token from the metadata server.
5. Other providers raise `InvokeError` unless `PSKIT_ENDPOINT_<NAME>` is set. Point it at the target's HTTP URL from `pskit info`. On Azure, invoke-only functions expose `POST /_pskit/invoke/<name>` (function key required).

Example: [`examples/09-function-invoke`](../examples/09-function-invoke).

Locally `invoke()` runs the other handler in-process. In the cloud, only AWS and GCP have a built-in way; on Azure it raises `InvokeError` unless `PSKIT_ENDPOINT_BILLING` is set [docs/handlers.md#invoke-calling-another-function].

Fix: set the endpoint to billing's URL. If `billing` is invoke-only, Azure gives it `POST /_pskit/invoke/billing`, which needs the function key.

**In code**
```yaml
stages:
  staging:
    functions:
      orders:
        environment:
          PSKIT_ENDPOINT_BILLING: ${env:BILLING_URL}
```
Set `BILLING_URL` from `pskit info -s staging` when you deploy. If the route needs the function key, include it the way Azure accepts it (for example a `code` query parameter in the URL), and treat that URL as a secret.

azure: storage trigger with events [created, deleted] on container uploads. supported?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/events.md#storage]
| azure | Blob trigger in the app's storage account | path pattern | **created/updated only**; container name 3–63 lowercase; `existing` buckets in another account need `options.storage_connection` |

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/providers.md#azure-azure-functions]
**Limits:** `auth: iam`/`jwt` aren't supported. `environment` is app-wide (warning on conflicting values). Timers ignore `timezone`. Blob `deleted` events aren't available. `fifo`, `dead_letter` and `topic.filter` aren't applied. Invoke-only functions (and task functions of native workflows) get `POST /_pskit/invoke/<name>` (function key).

No. Azure blob triggers fire on **created/updated** blobs only; `deleted` isn't available, and `pskit validate` reports `Azure blob triggers only fire on created/updated blobs` [docs/events.md#storage] [docs/providers.md#azure-azure-functions].

Options:
1. Keep `events: [created]` on Azure (the default).
2. If you also deploy elsewhere, keep `[created, deleted]` in the base file and override only Azure:
```yaml
providers:
  azure:
    functions:
      on-upload:
        events:
          - storage: {bucket: uploads, events: [created]}
```
Lists replace, so on Azure the function gets just this trigger.
3. If you need delete handling on Azure, have the code that deletes blobs publish a message to a queue or topic, and trigger a function from that.

Container names must be 3–63 lowercase characters.

Environment: provider=gcp stage=dev mode=ask page=Functions
We want searchable logs in Cloud Logging: each order log line should carry order_id and amount as fields, and the worker function should log at DEBUG while the others stay at INFO. How?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/handlers.md#logging]
## Logging

```python
ctx.logger.info("order created", extra={"order_id": 42, "amount": 9.5})
```

Output is one JSON object per line, which every cloud's log service can index:

```json
{"ts": "2026-01-01T12:00:00+00:00", "level": "INFO", "logger": "pskit.function", "message": "order created",
 "function": "create-order", "request_id": "…", "provider": "aws", "order_id": 42, "amount": 9.5}
```

`extra` keys that collide with Python `LogRecord` attributes (`name`, `message`, `msg`, `args`, …) are renamed with a trailing underscore (`name_`), so a log call can never crash your handler. For each HTTP request the runtime also logs method, path, status and duration.

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/handlers.md#environment-variables]
Runtime switches you can set:

| Variable | Effect |
|---|---|
| `PSKIT_LOG_FORMAT` | `json` (default in the cloud) or `text` (default under the CLI) |
| `PSKIT_LOG_LEVEL` / `LOG_LEVEL` | log level, default `INFO` |
| `PSKIT_DEBUG` | `1`/`true` adds exception details to 500 responses |

Use `ctx.logger` with `extra`: each call becomes one JSON object per line with your fields, which Cloud Logging can index [docs/handlers.md#logging]. The level comes from `PSKIT_LOG_LEVEL` (default `INFO`) [docs/handlers.md#environment-variables].

**In code**
```python
ctx.logger.info("order created", extra={"order_id": order["id"], "amount": order["amount"]})
```
```yaml
functions:
  worker:
    handler: app.worker.handle
    environment:
      PSKIT_LOG_LEVEL: DEBUG
```

**In studio**
1. Open **Functions** and click `worker`.
2. In the *Logging* section, set *Log level* to `DEBUG`.
3. Click **Save**.

The other functions keep the default `INFO`.

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/handlers.md#batchresult]
## `BatchResult`

Return a `BatchResult` from queue/topic/storage handlers to report the records that failed:

```python
from py_serverless_kit import BatchResult

def worker(event, ctx):
    result = BatchResult()
    for record in event.records:
        try:
            process(record.json())
        except Exception:
            result.fail(record)        # or result.fail(record.id)
    return result                      # BatchResult.of(failed_records) also works
```

| Provider | Behaviour |

Both. `result.fail(record)` or `result.fail(record.id)`, and `BatchResult.of(failed_records)` builds one from a list [docs/handlers.md#batchresult]. On SQS it becomes `batchItemFailures`, so only those messages are retried.

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/handlers.md#get_secret-secrets-on-every-provider]
## `get_secret()`: secrets on every provider

```python
from py_serverless_kit import get_secret, get_secrets, put_secret, SecretNotFound

password = get_secret("db-password")                 # plain secret
webhook = get_secret("stripe", "webhook")            # one field of a JSON secret
token = get_secret("optional-token", default="")     # no SecretNotFound
put_secret("last-run", "2026-10-22")                 # Vault / OpenBao and Secrets Manager
```

The store comes from environment variables, so the code does not change: `PSKIT_SECRETS_DRIVER` = `vault`
(HashiCorp Vault / OpenBao, with `PSKIT_SECRETS_URL` and `_TOKEN`), `aws` (AWS Secrets Manager; Lambda's credentials)
or `env` (default: `PSKIT_SECRET_<NAME>`, then `<NAME>`). `store="other"` reads `PSKIT_OTHER_*`. Values are cached for
60 s. On premises a one-click OpenBao, Secrets Manager compatible server or LocalStack writes these variables for you:
[resource-guides/onprem/secrets.md](resource-guides/onprem/secrets.md).

Right, never the literal key in `pskit.yml`. Read it with `get_secret()`; the store comes from environment variables, so the code doesn't change between clouds [docs/handlers.md#get_secret-secrets-on-every-provider].

**In code**
```python
from __future__ import annotations

from py_serverless_kit import get_secret


def charge(event, ctx):
    stripe_key = get_secret("stripe-api-key")
    return {"ok": bool(stripe_key)}
```
With the default `env` store it reads `PSKIT_SECRET_STRIPE_API_KEY`, then `STRIPE_API_KEY`. Pass it from your shell when you deploy:
```yaml
functions:
  charge:
    handler: app.handlers.charge
    environment:
      STRIPE_API_KEY: ${env:STRIPE_API_KEY}
```

messages.content:
[docs/placement.md#functions-on-several-servers-on-premises]
# Functions on several servers (on premises)

By default every function of a project runs in one host: on one machine, or on every server of a
[cluster](cluster.md). **Placement** splits them: each group of functions runs on its own server (or cluster),
with only its own code and dependencies, and the groups work together as one project.

[docs/placement.md#how-the-groups-work-together]
## How the groups work together

Every group is an independent host. Each one knows where every function lives and calls the others over HTTP
with a shared secret (`.pskit/onprem-<stage>/peer-token`, out of git):

| You do | What happens |
|---|---|
| `invoke("resize", data)` in a function on `api` | runs on `gpu`, the result (or the error, with its type) comes back |
| an HTTP request to `api` for a route of `resize` | `404` with the URL on `gpu` (each server answers only its own routes); with `placement.gateway: true` (on by default behind a load balancer that reaches both groups) `api` passes it to `gpu` |

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/studio.md#test-functions]
## Test functions

The **Test** page (or **Test** on a function row) sends events to a function:

1. Pick the function and the event: one of its triggers (HTTP, schedule, queue, storage, topic) or **Direct invoke**.
2. Edit the payload. It starts from a sample for that trigger type (a storage sample matches the trigger's prefix and
   suffix; a schedule uses its own `input`). **Save event** keeps named payloads per function in
   `.pskit/studio/test-events.json`, like test events in the Lambda console.
3. **Run locally** runs the handler on this machine with a synthetic event (`pskit invoke`): no cloud, no deploy.
   **Send to <provider>/<stage>** fires the real trigger of the deployed function (`pskit trigger`): a queue message,
   an uploaded object, a topic message, an HTTP request or an invocation. Turn on *Show the function's logs* to watch it.

[docs/cli.md#pskit-trigger]
pskit trigger -f worker -e 0 -d '{"order_id": 1}'      # trigger #0 of worker, e.g. an SQS message
pskit trigger -f worker -e 0 -d '[{"id": 1}, {"id": 2}]'   # two queue messages

**In studio**
1. **Test**: pick `worker` and its queue trigger in *1. Choose the event*.
2. *2. Edit the event*: change the sample payload, e.g. `{"order_id": 1}`.
3. *3. Run it*: press **☁ Send to On-premises / prod**. Turn on *Show the function's logs* to watch it run [docs/studio.md#test-functions].

**In the terminal**
```bash
pskit trigger -f worker -e 0 -d '{"order_id": 1}' -s prod
pskit logs -f --function worker -s prod
```
`-e 0` is the first trigger of `worker` [docs/cli.md#pskit-trigger].

I'd like to run pskit studio on a build server and open it from my laptop's browser. Is that safe, and what's the recommended way?

function.name: search_docs
function.arguments: {"query": "studio host bind remote access security token"}

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/studio.md#security]
## Security

Studio can write files in the project and run deploys with your cloud credentials, so:

- It binds to `127.0.0.1` by default.
- Every API call needs the session token from the printed URL. Anyone who has that URL has full access, so don't share
  it. A new token is generated each time studio starts.
- Requests with a foreign `Host` header (DNS rebinding) or a cross-site `Origin` are refused, and bodies are capped at 2 MiB.

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/studio.md#studio-build-a-project-without-writing-yaml]
| `--host` | `127.0.0.1` | Bind address. Anything other than loopback prints a warning: studio can edit files and deploy |

Be careful with this. Studio can write files in the project and run deploys with that server's cloud credentials. Anyone who has the URL with its session token gets full access [docs/studio.md#security].

Safest way: keep studio on loopback (the default) and forward the port over SSH.
```bash
pskit studio --port 8770
```
Then on your laptop:
```bash
ssh -L 8770:127.0.0.1:8770 me@build.example.com
```
Open the URL studio prints (it ends with the session token) in your laptop's browser.

`pskit studio --host 0.0.0.0` also works, but it prints a warning, because studio would then be reachable from the network [docs/studio.md#studio-build-a-project-without-writing-yaml]. Don't share the token URL. A new token is generated each time studio starts.

Our lab server only allows password SSH logins and I'm on Linux. How do I save it in pskit without writing the password anywhere in the project?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resource-guides/onprem/services.md#ssh-login-key-agent-or-password]
## SSH login: key, agent or password

The *SSH server* target (and `provider.options.deploy` for the functions) logs in one of three ways:

| *Log in with* | Studio | CLI | `pskit.yml` (`provider.options.deploy`) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Key file** | path of the `.pem` / private key | `--pem ~/.ssh/server.pem` | `pem: ~/.ssh/server.pem` |
| **SSH agent / default key** | nothing to fill in | leave `--pem` out | leave `pem` out, or `auth: agent` |
| **Password** | the password (saved in `.pskit/ssh/`, owner-only, out of git) | `--ssh-password-env VAR` or `--ssh-password-file FILE` | `password_file: ~/.ssh/server.pass`, or `auth: password` with `SSHPASS` set |

*SSH agent / default key* is what `ssh user@host` does in a terminal: the agent, `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` /
`id_rsa`, and `~/.ssh/config` (`Host` aliases, `IdentityFile`, jump hosts).

Password logins go through **sshpass**, so the password never appears on a command line or in the state. Install it

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resource-guides/onprem/services.md#servers-several-machines]
pskit resources onprem servers add lab --ssh root@192.168.1.20 --ssh-password-env LAB_PW --sudo

Install `sshpass` and pass the password through an environment variable [docs/resource-guides/onprem/services.md#ssh-login-key-agent-or-password].

**In the terminal**
```bash
export LAB_PW='<password>'
pskit resources onprem servers add lab --ssh root@192.0.2.60 --ssh-password-env LAB_PW --sudo
pskit resources onprem servers test lab
```
A typed password goes to `.pskit/ssh/` (owner-only), never to pskit.yml or a command line [docs/resource-guides/onprem/services.md#ssh-login-key-agent-or-password]. The server must allow `PasswordAuthentication`.

Long term, a key is simpler: `pskit resources onprem ssh-key root@192.0.2.60` installs one with the password once.

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resources.md#what-handlers-receive]
## What handlers receive

For each resource bound to a function:

```
PSKIT_RESOURCES=uploads,jobs
PSKIT_RESOURCE_UPLOADS_TYPE=storage
PSKIT_RESOURCE_UPLOADS_NAME=acme-uploads-1234     # resolved native name
PSKIT_RESOURCE_UPLOADS_EXTERNAL=false
PSKIT_RESOURCE_UPLOADS_<KEY>=...                  # one per connection entry
PSKIT_RESOURCE_UPLOADS_ARN / _URL / _ID=...       # when the provider knows them
```

`<KEY>` is the key with every non-alphanumeric character replaced by `_`, in upper case (`orders-db` → `ORDERS_DB`). A `connection` entry wins over a provider value with the same name.

| Provider | Values added |
|---|---|
| aws | `ARN` for storage, queue and topic. Queues also get `URL`. External resources bound by name are looked up with a Terraform data source. With `connection.arn`, that ARN is used as-is |
| gcp | `ID` for managed queues and topics (the Pub/Sub topic id) |
| others | only `TYPE`, `NAME`, `EXTERNAL` and your `connection` values |

Added an external cache:

```yaml
resources:
  cache:
    type: cache
    external: true
    connection:
      url: redis://cache.example.com:6379/0
    functions: [api]
```
Validate for onprem: valid. pskit doesn't create or change that Redis; it only passes the connection to `api` [docs/resources.md#what-handlers-receive]. Your handler still needs a Redis client (add `redis` to `requirements.txt`).

If that Redis needs a password, don't put it in the URL here: give me the variable name and I'll use `${env:NAME}`.

messages.content:
Done. `weekend-message` runs every Friday at 17:00 London time and posts "Have a nice weekend, everyone!" to your chat.

messages.name: get_project

service: shop
provider:
  name: onprem
  region: local
  options:
    port: 8324
functions:
  validate-cart:
    handler: app.steps.validate_cart
  reserve-stock:
    handler: app.steps.reserve_stock
  charge-card:
    handler: app.steps.charge_card
  send-receipt:
    handler: app.steps.send_receipt
workflows:
  place-order:
    start_at: validate
    states:
      validate: {type: task, function: validate-cart, next: charge}
      charge:
        type: task
        function: charge-card
        next: receipt
        retry: [{errors: ["*"], max_attempts: 3, interval_seconds: 5}]
      receipt: {type: task, function: send-receipt, end: true}
files:
app/__init__.py
app/steps.py

```yaml
workflows:
  place-order:
    states:
      validate: {type: task, function: validate-cart, next: reserve}
      reserve: {type: task, function: reserve-stock, next: charge}
```

`charge` and its retry are unchanged.

Checks:
- `pskit validate` (onprem, staging): valid (embedded engine).
- `reserve-stock` with `{"cart": "C-1"}`: `{"cart": "C-1", "reserved": true}`.

Run the whole flow locally: `pskit workflow run place-order -i '{"cart": "C-1"}' --history`, or on **Deploy > Run a workflow locally**. The **Workflows** page shows the new box between validate and charge. Deploy: **Deploy** page or `pskit deploy -s staging`.

### State: remote Terraform backend

By default Terraform state lives in `.pskit/<provider>-<stage>/terraform.tfstate`, which is git-ignored. For teams and CI, use a remote backend:

```yaml
provider:
  state:
    backend: s3                      # any terraform backend type: s3, gcs, azurerm, http, remote, ...

      key: orders/${opt:stage}.tfstate
```

curl: (7) Failed to connect to 192.0.2.10 port 8080: Connection refused

but pskit logs and the Test page work fine for this server

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/providers.md#onprem-on-premises]
**Ports closed to this machine.** The host binds `127.0.0.1` on the server unless `options.host: 0.0.0.0`, and cloud firewalls often block 8080. When the host's port cannot be opened from here, pskit sends the control call (logs, triggers, uploads, HTTP tests) over the deploy's SSH login to `127.0.0.1:<port>` on the server, with the admin token on stdin rather than on a command line. To call the functions from other machines, still open the port (`options.host: 0.0.0.0` plus the firewall rule) or use `pskit client tunnel`.

The host listens only on `127.0.0.1` on the server, which is the default. pskit itself still works because it goes over SSH to `127.0.0.1:<port>` when it can't reach the port [docs/providers.md#onprem-on-premises].

**In code**
```yaml
provider:
  name: onprem
  options:
    host: 0.0.0.0
    port: 8080
```
Deploy again, and allow TCP 8080 in the server's firewall. If you only need access from your own machine, `pskit client tunnel` forwards the port over SSH instead.

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resource-guides/onprem/services.md#where-a-server-is-used-and-how-the-servers-connect]
The **Network map** page draws every server and the connections it has to accept (inbound) and open (outbound):
this machine (SSH, logs, tests), the function callers, the cluster ports, load balancer → servers, replicas → primary,
functions → services, downloads from the internet. Solid lines are required, dashed ones are needed for a feature,
dotted ones are optional (pskit falls back to an SSH tunnel). Click a server for its inbound and outbound ports, why
each is needed, and where it is used. It reads the same rules as `pskit firewall`, from local files only.

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/onprem-network.md#network-and-firewall-rules-on-premises]
**You do not have to work these out by hand.** Every step prints the rules it just made necessary, with your
servers' names and addresses and `ufw` commands: `pskit cluster create`, `pskit cluster join`, `pskit deploy`
(one server, function groups or a cluster), `pskit lb create`, `pskit lb attach`, `pskit cluster balancer set`,
a project's `balancer` route, and `pskit resources onprem create`. `pskit firewall` lists everything the project
needs now, per server (`--server edge2`, `--json`); the studio shows the same in a **Firewall** panel (Deploy,
cluster and load balancer pages) and in each job's output:

You don't have to do anything there. It's a map that helps you open the right firewall ports.

The **Network map** draws every saved server and the connections it must accept (inbound) and open (outbound): SSH from this machine, callers of your functions, cluster ports, load balancer to servers, functions to services, and downloads [docs/resource-guides/onprem/services.md#where-a-server-is-used-and-how-the-servers-connect].
- Solid line: required
- Dashed line: needed for a feature
- Dotted line: optional (pskit falls back to an SSH tunnel)

**In studio**
1. Open **Network map**.
2. Click a server to see its inbound and outbound ports, why each one is needed, and where the server is used.

**In the terminal**
```bash
pskit firewall
pskit firewall --server app-1
```
`pskit firewall` lists the same rules per server, and deploy, cluster and load balancer commands print them too [docs/onprem-network.md#network-and-firewall-rules-on-premises]. The map reads local files only and doesn't contact your servers.

[docs/providers.md#onprem-on-premises]
**Deploy targets** (`options.deploy`)

| `method` | What runs | Target needs | Laptop needs |
|---|---|---|---|
| `local` (default) | detached process on this machine | Python (the interpreter that runs `pskit`) | — |
| `ssh` or `scp` | one `release.tar.gz` extracted on the server, then a process or a systemd unit. Apply runs `systemctl restart` and waits for `/__pskit/health` | SSH. Python only if `python: system`. Passwordless `sudo` when `install: systemd` and `sudo: true` | OpenSSH (`ssh`, `scp`). Optional `.pem` |
| `docker` | image built on this machine, then `docker load` + `docker run` on the server. Apply waits until the container answers `/__pskit/health` | SSH. Docker is installed at apply when it is missing (`install_docker: true`, the default). Passwordless `sudo` when the daemon must be installed or the user cannot talk to it | Docker CLI, OpenSSH. Optional `.pem` |

company give me an existing resource group, i not allowed create new. where put it, in gui

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/providers.md#azure-azure-functions]
- **Credentials:** `az login` + `ARM_SUBSCRIPTION_ID`, or service principal env vars
- **Dependencies:** remote Oryx build from `requirements.txt` (`azure-functions` is added automatically); Node.js: from `package.json` (`@azure/functions` v4 is added)
- **Node.js:** `nodejs18`, `nodejs20`, `nodejs22` → `application_stack.node_version` `18` / `20` / `22`. Generated `pskit_entry.js` (the package's `main`) uses the v4 programming model: one `app.http()` / `app.timer()` / `app.storageQueue()` / `app.storageBlob()` / `app.serviceBusTopic()` per trigger, the same function names and routes as `function_app.py`, including the `_pskit/invoke/<fn>` routes for invoke-only and Logic Apps task functions. Several `Set-Cookie` headers are all kept (Python keeps only the last)

```yaml
provider:
  name: azure
  region: westeurope
  options:
    subscription_id: ${env:ARM_SUBSCRIPTION_ID}   # or the env var itself
    resource_group: existing-rg                   # optional: use an existing resource group
    plan_sku: Y1                                  # default Y1 (Consumption)
    app_insights: true                            # default true
    storage_connection: OTHER_STORAGE             # app setting name, for `existing` queues/buckets in another account
    servicebus_namespace_id: /subscriptions/.../namespaces/my-sb   # for `existing` topics
    servicebus_connection: SB_CONNECTION                          # app setting with its connection string
```

One **Linux Consumption Function App** hosts every function of a service, using the Python v2 programming model: pskit generates `function_app.py` and `host.json`. `routePrefix` is empty, so your paths are served exactly as configured (no `/api`). `{path+}` becomes Azure's `{*path}`.

**In studio**
1. **Overview & provider**: open *Azure Functions options*.
2. Type the group's name in **Resource group** (empty means pskit creates one).
3. **Save**, then **Deploy > Deploy**.

two secret stores: openbao 'secrets' and aws-compatible 'aws-secrets'. how do I pick the store in get_secret?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resource-guides/onprem/secrets.md#one-click-openbao-pskits-secrets-manager-or-localstack]
Name it **`secrets`** and handlers need no `store=`: it is the default store. Another key works too:
`get_secret("db-password", store="aws-secrets")` / `getSecret("db-password", { store: "aws-secrets" })`.

The store keyed `secrets` is the default, so `get_secret("db-password")` reads OpenBao. For the other one, pass `store=` [docs/resource-guides/onprem/secrets.md#one-click-openbao-pskits-secrets-manager-or-localstack]:

```python
from __future__ import annotations

from py_serverless_kit import get_secret


def handler(event, ctx):
    db = get_secret("db-password")
    legacy = get_secret("db-password", store="aws-secrets")
    return {"same": db == legacy}
```
Node.js: `getSecret("db-password", { store: "aws-secrets" })`.

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resources.md#troubleshooting]
| `function 'x' has a queue event on resource 'y', which is a storage` | the resource `type` must match the event kind |

The event kind must match the resource's `type` [docs/resources.md#troubleshooting]. `uploads` is a storage resource, so use a storage event:

```yaml
functions:
  ingest:
    handler: app.handlers.ingest
    events:
      - storage: {resource: uploads}
```
If you really want a queue, add a separate `type: queue` resource and point the queue event at it.

Timesheets send start and end as HH:MM. Day shifts are fine, but the night shift from 22:00 to 06:00 comes out as -16 hours. It should be 8. Shifts are never longer than 24 hours.

With only HH:MM, both times are on the same (dummy) day, so 06:00 is before 22:00 and the difference is negative. An end at or before the start now means the next day.

Environment: provider=onprem stage=prod mode=ask page=Resources

Files land in an Azure Blob container from a partner. Our processing functions run on our own servers. Can the on-prem host watch that container and trigger a function per new blob? Which values do I need?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resource-guides/onprem/storage.md#a-bucket-in-a-cloud]
## A bucket in a cloud

| Bucket | Driver | Required | Where to find the values |
|---|---|---|---|
| Amazon S3 | `aws` | `region` (+ `access_key_env` / `secret_key_env`, or `AWS_*` on the host) | S3 console → bucket → *Properties → AWS Region*; IAM access key |
| Cloudflare R2 | `r2` | `account_id`, `access_key_env`, `secret_key_env` | [cloudflare/storage.md](../cloudflare/storage.md#2-collect-the-values) (*Manage R2 API Tokens*) |
| Azure Blob | `azure_blob` | `connection_string_env` (or `account` + key / SAS), `container` | [azure/storage.md](../azure/storage.md#2-collect-the-values) |
| Google Cloud Storage | `gcs` | `token_command` or `access_token_env` | bucket name from the Cloud Storage console |

Yes. Declare the container as an external storage resource with the `azure_blob` driver. The host polls it and each new blob triggers your function like a local event [docs/resource-guides/onprem/storage.md#a-bucket-in-a-cloud].

You need `connection_string_env` (or `account` plus a key or SAS) and the `container`.

**In code**
```yaml
resources:
  partner-files:
    type: storage
    external: true
    options:
      driver: azure_blob
      connection_string_env: AZURE_STORAGE_CONNECTION_STRING
      container: partner-drop
functions:
  process:
    handler: app.handlers.process
    events:
      - storage: {resource: partner-files, events: [created]}
```
Put `AZURE_STORAGE_CONNECTION_STRING` in the host's env file (`provider.options.env_file`), not in pskit.yml.

**In studio**
1. Open **Resources** > **+ Add resource**, *Type* storage, *External / existing*.
2. Under *On-prem driver*, pick Azure Blob and fill in its fields. Secret fields can read an environment variable.
3. Add a *Storage* trigger on it in **Functions**, then **Save**.

Blobs already in the container at the first start are recorded, not emitted.

Environment: provider=azure stage=prod mode=ask page=Workflows
our azure logic app workflow (engine native) runs 5 minutes. the start request returns an error after about 2 min, but the run finishes fine

function.name: search_docs
function.arguments: {"query": "logic apps synchronous response 2 minutes sync false"}

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/workflows.md#compiler-notes-and-limits]
- **Azure (Logic Apps):** the state machine runs as an interpreter: an `Until` loop over a `Switch` on the current state, with the data kept as a JSON string variable. The HTTP trigger answers with the output (`200`) or `{"error", "cause"}` (`500`); a synchronous `Response` must come within about 2 minutes, so set `options.sync: false` for long workflows. Only the **first** retry rule of a task is used, as Logic Apps' exponential retry policy (it retries 408/429/5xx responses: the `errors` filter and `backoff_rate` are ignored, intervals are 5 s–1 day, at most 90 retries). `retry`/`catch` work on `task` states only. Task calls time out after 120 s (the Logic Apps limit for outbound HTTP), and `pskit validate` warns when a task function's timeout is longer. `map` iterations run one at a time (`max_concurrency` is ignored). `matches` accepts `abc`, `abc*`, `*abc`, `*abc*` and `*`; other globs are a validation error. `is_present` treats `null` like a missing key. `result_path` can't contain array indexes. Logic Apps allow 8 levels of nesting, so `parallel` states can nest at most three deep and `map` states two deep. A run stops after 5000 states or `timeout` (default 1 hour).

The HTTP trigger answers synchronously with the output, and that response must come within about 2 minutes. For long workflows set `options.sync: false` [docs/workflows.md#compiler-notes-and-limits].

**In code**
```yaml
workflows:
  order-pipeline:
    engine: native
    options:
      sync: false
```
Then the start call no longer waits for the result.

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/handlers.md#httprequest]
| `headers` | `Headers`: case-insensitive, read-only mapping; repeated headers joined with `", "` |

Both values in one string, joined with `", "`, for example `"a, b"`. `headers` is case-insensitive, so `x-tag` and `X-Tag` both work [docs/handlers.md#httprequest].

```python
tags = [t.strip() for t in event.http.headers.get("x-tag", "").split(",") if t.strip()]
```

Environment: provider=onprem stage=staging mode=auto page=YAML
redis queue driver: url vs url_env, which one keeps the password out of the generated files?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resource-guides/onprem/queue.md#3-declare-it-in-pskityml]
### 3. Declare it in `pskit.yml`

```yaml
resources:
  jobs:
    type: queue
    external: true
    options:
      driver: redis
      url_env: REDIS_URL         # or url: redis://... (then it's written into the generated files)
      key: jobs

functions:
  worker:
    handler: app.handlers.work
    events:
      - queue: {resource: jobs, batch_size: 10, visibility_timeout: 60}
```

Other producers can `LPUSH jobs '<text>'`; plain strings are delivered as the record body. How messages are leased:

[docs/resource-guides/onprem/README.md#secrets-name_env]
## Secrets: `<name>_env`

Any driver parameter can be written as `<name>_env: VARIABLE` instead of `<name>: value`:

```yaml
options:
  driver: minio
  endpoint: http://minio.internal:9000
  access_key_env: MINIO_ACCESS_KEY     # read from the HOST's environment when it starts
  secret_key_env: MINIO_SECRET_KEY
```

The host reads `VARIABLE` from its own environment at start, so the secret never lands in Terraform state or
`pskit_host.json`. A missing variable stops the host with an error naming it.

`url_env`. With `url: redis://...` the value is written into the generated files. With `url_env: REDIS_URL` the host reads the variable from its own environment at start, so it never lands in Terraform state or `pskit_host.json` [docs/resource-guides/onprem/README.md#secrets-name_env].

**In code**
```yaml
resources:
  jobs:
    type: queue
    external: true
    options:
      driver: redis
      url_env: REDIS_URL
      key: jobs
```
Every driver parameter works this way (`<name>_env: VARIABLE`). If the variable is missing on the host, the host stops with an error that names it [docs/resource-guides/onprem/queue.md#3-declare-it-in-pskityml].

the ssh server dont have python and i cant install it. just yaml pls

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/providers.md#onprem-on-premises]
When the server has **no Python**, use `python: bundle` (a portable CPython from [python-build-standalone](https://github.com/astral-sh/python-build-standalone) is fetched at apply and copied with the app) or `method: docker` (the image is `FROM python:<minor>-slim`). From Windows, a Linux bundle is copied out of the downloaded archive and is not unpacked into the project (those trees contain test paths longer than `MAX_PATH`). Air-gapped: `python_home` (copy a tree you already have) or `python_url` + `python_sha256` (internal mirror of an `install_only` tarball).

**In code**
```yaml
provider:
  name: onprem
  options:
    deploy:
      method: ssh
      host: 192.0.2.10
      user: pskit
      path: /opt/pskit/orders
      python: bundle
```
With `python: bundle` a portable CPython is fetched at apply and copied with the app [docs/providers.md#onprem-on-premises].

Hi

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/studio.md#what-you-can-do]
| **Functions** | A table of functions and a four-step **Create function** wizard like the AWS Lambda console: basics, triggers, environment & permissions, review (a YAML diff). Trigger types the selected provider can't run are disabled, with a tooltip naming the providers that can. HTTP has a path-parameter preview, CORS and auth. Schedule has rate presets and a cron editor with a plain-English preview. Queue/storage/topic can be **new**, a **resource** from the Resources page, **Browse account** (lists what already exists in your cloud), or a typed name. Creating a function writes a handler stub into your code |

**In studio**
1. **Functions**: click the `report` row.
2. Go to the **Triggers** step and, under *Add a trigger*, click **Schedule**.
3. In **Run** pick *At a specific time*, **Repeat** = *Every day*, **At** = `06:00`. The help line shows the cron it writes (`0 6 * * *`).
4. Optional: choose your **Timezone** (GCP supports it).
5. **Apply changes**, **Save**, then **Deploy > Deploy**.

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/troubleshooting.md#security-notes]
- Created AWS buckets block public access. Prefer a least-privilege `iam.statements` over `"*"` resources.

Buckets pskit creates on AWS block public access [docs/troubleshooting.md#security-notes], and pskit.yml has no key to open them. That's on purpose: a public bucket lets anyone list and download everything in it.

Safer: give customers short-lived links. Add an HTTP function that checks the customer, then returns a presigned URL from boto3 (`generate_presigned_url`, for example 15 minutes). Its role needs `s3:GetObject` on the bucket in `iam.statements`.

Browse account on GCP shows a message instead of my buckets. what does it need?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/studio.md#browse-account]
## Browse account

**Browse account** lists queues, buckets, topics and state machines that already exist, so you pick one instead of
typing its name. It runs with the credentials of the machine running studio:

| Provider | Lists | Needs |
|---|---|---|
| AWS | SQS queues, S3 buckets, SNS topics, Step Functions state machines | `pip install "py-serverless-kit[aws]"`, AWS credentials |
| GCP | Pub/Sub topics and subscriptions, Cloud Storage buckets | `google-cloud-pubsub` / `google-cloud-storage`, `provider.options.project` or `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT` |
| Azure | Storage queues and blob containers | `azure-storage-queue` / `azure-storage-blob`, `AZURE_STORAGE_CONNECTION_STRING` |
| On premises | Existing queue and bucket directories under the host's data directory | nothing |
| Others | Not available | type the name |

A missing SDK or credential shows a message in the picker; you can always type the name instead.

On GCP, **Browse account** lists Pub/Sub topics and subscriptions and Cloud Storage buckets. It needs [docs/studio.md#browse-account]:
1. The SDKs on the machine running studio:
```bash
pip install google-cloud-pubsub google-cloud-storage
```
2. The project: `provider.options.project`, or `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT`.
3. Credentials on that machine, for example `gcloud auth application-default login`.

Restart studio after installing the packages if it still shows the message. You can always type the bucket name instead.

Cause: `render`'s role only has what pskit grants for its own trigger (the queue); nothing allows reading the design team's bucket.

```yaml
functions:
```
